cognate: Ved. āmá- 'raw' = Gk ὠμός (*h₂oh₃mó-); Ved. kravís- 'raw flesh' = Gk κρέας (*krewh₂-s); Ved. ad- = Gk ἔδ- (ἔδμεναι, -ηστής, ἐδεστής) (*h₁ed- 'eat')
drift_or_renewal: Vedic keeps kravís- as a marked word for raw/gory flesh and builds the verb phrase into agent compounds (āmā́d-, kravyā́d-); Greek uses the ordinary κρέας 'meat' and builds parallel agent formations ὠμηστής, κρεῶν ἐδεστής (parallel compounding, not an exact equation: suffixes differ). AVŚ 8.6.48 renews the noun once with māṃsa- (āmaṃ māṃsam) beside kraviḥ.
shared_syntax: verb 'eat' + object noun phrase 'raw flesh' (adj. *h₂oh₃mo- + noun *krewh₂-): Ved. āmásya kravíṣaḥ (RV 1.162.10), āmaṃ māṃsam adanti ... kraviḥ (AVŚ 8.6.48) ~ Gk ὤμ̓ ... κρέα ἔδμεναι (Il. 22.347), κρεῶν ἐδεστὰς ὠμῶν (Hdt.); plus agentive 'raw-eater' formations on both sides
context: The AV anchor is a charm against demons who eat raw (human, pauruṣeya-) flesh; RV 10.87.16 has the same 'human flesh' (paúruṣeyeṇa kravíṣā) of the yātudhāna, and kravyā́d-/āmā́d- name corpse-eating demons and the corpse-eating fire. Greek congruence is in the support, not the slab anchor: the Hippocratic anchor is prose in a dietary register (raw vs boiled meat) and only witnesses the cognate pair ὠμός + κρέας. In epic, eating raw flesh is the mark of the savage and of corpse-devourers: Achilles' wish to eat Hector raw (Il. 22.347), dogs and birds as ὠμησταί tearing the unburied dead (Il. 11.454, 22.67), Achilles as ὠμηστὴς ἀνήρ (Il. 24.207); Herodotus' cannibal Padaioi are κρεῶν ἐδεσταὶ ὠμῶν. Both traditions put 'eating raw flesh' on demons/beasts that devour human bodies. Caveat: 'eat raw meat' can be formed independently from ordinary words, which keeps this from high; what argues for inheritance is that all three lexemes are cognate, the context (devouring human corpses) agrees, and both sides derive agent nouns from the phrase.
phrase: *h₂oh₃mó- *krewh₂- *h₁ed- 'eat raw flesh' — Ved. āmaṃ ... adanti ... kraviḥ ~ Gk ὠμῶν κρεῶν; ὤμ̓ ... κρέα ἔδμεναι

cognate: Gk ἴς = Lat. uīs (*wiH-s 'force'); Gk ἄνεμος 'wind' ~ Lat. anima 'breath, air' (*h₂enh₁-mo- / *h₂enh₁-meh₂-, same root and suffix, different stem class)
drift_or_renewal: drift: ἄνεμος means 'wind', anima mostly 'breath, life-spirit' (3.397 uis animai = force of the soul), but in Lucr. 6.578, 6.592 and 5.1230 anima still means moving air or wind, so the drift is partial. Renewal: the commoner Latin form is uis uenti, with uentus in place of anima.
shared_syntax: head noun *wiHs + dependent genitive of *h₂enh₁-mo-/-meh₂ 'wind/air': ἲς ἀνέμου/ἀνέμοιο ~ animae uis / uis animai
context: Homer's ἲς ἀνέμοιο is formulaic (5 times), always the force of wind driving waves or ships; Hesiod's ἲς ἀνέμου Βορέου is the winter north wind. In Lucr. 6.578 animae uis is wind/air pent up in the earth that causes earthquakes, set next to uentus; 6.592 couples impetus animai and uis uenti. The AV pivots in B-7bb5a/B-f8529 (AVŚ 6.10.2 prāṇa beside vāyu; AVŚ 5.9.8 vātaḥ prāṇaḥ 'wind is breath') pair the same root with 'wind', but as lists, not a syntagm, so they are not anchors. This is low because uis + genitive is Lucretius' default idiom (uis animi, uis uenti, ...), and Lucretius knew Homer, so the Latin phrase may be imitation or independent; the only evidence for inheritance is the cognate pair *wiHs + *h₂enh₁-mo- 'force of the wind'.
phrase: *wiHs *h₂enh₁mo- (gen.) 'force of the wind': ἲς ἀνέμου ~ animae uis

cognate: Ved. ákṣita- = Gk ἄφθιτος (*n̥-dʰgʷʰi-tó-); Ved. útsa- 'spring' (*ud-s-o-) and Gk ὕδωρ (*wód-r̥) are both built on the root *wed-/ud- 'water'
drift_or_renewal: the noun is renewed by suffix: útsa- (s-stem derivative) vs ὕδωρ (r/n-stem), same root; meaning drifts from 'not running dry, inexhaustible' (of a spring that is milked) to 'imperishable' (of the Styx's primeval water)
shared_syntax: attributive adjective *n̥-dʰgʷʰi-to- + noun for a water source/water (accusative object in Vedic, nominative apposition in Greek)
context: In the Vedic texts útsam ákṣitam is formulaic: the Maruts pour or milk the never-failing spring (AVŚ 4.27.3, RV 1.64.6, 8.7.16; also of wells and the Soma stream). The Greek slab anchor gives only the adjective, with another noun (ἄφθιτα μήδεα of Zeus); the water collocation exists in Greek only once, at Hes. Th. 805 Στυγὸς ἄφθιτον ὕδωρ (in support). What lifts it above chance pairing of a common adjective with 'water' is that útsa- and ὕδωρ share the root *wed-. It is weakened by the single Greek attestation and by how freely ἄφθιτος and ákṣita- combine with other nouns. The link between ákṣiti of streams and the κλέος ἄφθιτον equation is from memory of the comparative literature (Nagy).

note: All 174 bundles read (mostly AV pivots with Greek prose partners; most hold nothing inherited). 3 claims: 1 medium (eat raw flesh), 2 low.
